title: "About `hmt-apps`"
---


## The HMT archive

Throughout the first quarter of the twenty-first century, the Homer Multitext project's (HMT) work on Homeric manuscripts intentionally prioritized building openly licensed data sets in simple plain-text formats over developing apps.  Major components of the archive include (among other things):

- collections of digital images of Homeric manuscripts
- cataloged data about manuscripts of the *Iliad*
- editions of texts of the *Iliad* and *scholia*
- indexes associating texts, manuscript pages, and images
- other indexes including proper nouns and adjectives

This fundamental decision about how to distribute its work is epitomized in the publication of the HMT archive in a single plain-text file, that is always available in its most recent release on [github, here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/homermultitext/hmt-archive/refs/heads/master/releases-cex/hmt-current.cex).


## "Two-coffee apps"

This repository is a personal project inspired by the potential of coding agents like Claude. Working with the HMT project's data releases constantly inspires new ideas for apps to explore the complex interrelationships in the HMT data. With an agentic assistant, it's now remarkably straightforward to draft working versions of these ideas very quickly. I developed each of the [apps linked here](./apps/) to a point where I was comfortable releasing it on github in less time than it took me to finish two cups of coffee. The initial investment in both time and coffee is small enough that if an idea doesn't work out, I can throw it away without hesitation. This dramatically accelerated release cycle gives new meaning to Eric Raymond's famous aphorism, "Release early, release often." By reducing the effort to build an app, coding agents can be a boon to scholars with expertise in particular subject matter, rather than in software engineering.

All of the apps in this repository start by downloading the HMT project's latest data release. Apps quickly developed by agents like Claude  amplify the value of the data, and offer a powerful new justification for the HMT project's decision to favor developing datasets over software.
